title: Quantum double lock-in detection via sequential orthogonal quantum mixing
authors: Min Zhuang, Sijie Chen, Jiahao Huang, Chaohong Lee
abstract: High-precision measurement of oscillating signal is a ubiquitous issue in fundamental science and a critical task in practical technologies. In quantum metrology, quantum lock-in detection provide an efficient method for measuring such signal. In general, when the initial phase of the oscillating signal is unknown,quantum double lock-in detection can effectively extract complete information about the signal's amplitude, frequency, and initial phase. Conventional quantum double lock-in detection requires two individual quantum interferometry, each of which must undergo state preparation and readout. However, the time for state preparation and readout need not be negligible in practical experiments. In particular, the time for state preparation is longer than the time for sensing. To save experimental resources, it is challenging to achieve quantum double lock-in detection just via a single quantum interferometry while still extracting complete information about the signal's amplitude, frequency, and initial phase. Here, we present a general protocol for achieving a quantum double lock-in detection just via a single quantum interferometry under a sequential orthogonal periodic multipulse sequences. In particular, if the input state is a Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger state and two interaction-based operations are applied during interferometry, the measurement precisions for frequency, amplitude, and initial phase can both approach the Heisenberg limit. Our study paves a new way for measuring oscillating signals with a single quantum interferometry, and provides a feasible method for achieving Heisenberg-limited detection of alternating signals.
summary: This paper presents a breakthrough protocol for quantum double lock-in detection, enabling the simultaneous measurement of a signal's amplitude, frequency, and phase using only one quantum interferometer. By employing sequential orthogonal pulses and utilizing entangled GHZ states, the technique achieves Heisenberg-limited precision, significantly surpassing classical and standard quantum limits.
main_problem: The paper addresses the challenge of achieving high-precision quantum double lock-in detection—which requires measuring signal amplitude, frequency, and initial phase—using minimal experimental resources.
main_result: A novel protocol using a single quantum interferometry, specifically with Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger (GHZ) states, allows measurement precisions to approach the Heisenberg limit ($\propto 1/N$).
method: The method involves a three-stage quantum sensing protocol: initialization, interrogation via sequential orthogonal periodic multipulse sequences (PDD and CP), and final readout.
model_or_system: The system is modeled using an ensemble of N two-state bosonic particles, described by collective spin operators ($\hat{J}_x, \hat{J}_y, \hat{J}_z$) and governed by a Hamiltonian incorporating the oscillating signal and reference pulses.
key_observables: The half-population difference $\langle J_z angle_f$ is the primary observable, analyzed via Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) or Inverse Participation Ratio (IPR) to locate the lock-in point.
important_parameters: The measurement precision scales with $N$ (particle number), aiming for the Heisenberg Limit ($1/N$) over the Standard Quantum Limit ($1/\sqrt{N}$).
main_assumptions: The protocol assumes the ability to execute ideal $\pi$-pulses and analyzes robustness against systematic detuning and rotation angle errors.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the three stages of the detection scheme. Figure 2 shows FFT/IPR spectra confirming lock-in detection. Figure 3 compares measurement precision scaling ($\Delta A, \Delta\omega, \Delta eta$) vs. $N$ for both individual and GHZ states. Figure 5 shows scaling under detection noise.
paper_structure: The paper first introduces the problem and the single-interferometry protocol. It details the mathematical framework using sequential pulses, analyzes the measurement observables (SCS vs. GHZ states), demonstrates the scaling improvement to the Heisenberg limit, and finally proves the scheme's robustness against common experimental noise sources.
why_interesting: This work is highly relevant to AMO physics and quantum optics as it proposes a resource-efficient, high-precision measurement technique for oscillating signals using collective spin systems (like trapped ions or atoms).
